model.question: In example 2 the sample proportion (0.19) was above the national figure (0.157), yet we did not reject $H_0$. Which statement best explains this?

choices.text: A sample proportion of 0.19 is not surprising when $p = 0.157$ and n = 100—the difference is within chance variation
choices.feedback: Correct! With $n = 100$, getting a sample proportion of 0.19 when the true proportion is 0.157 is not surprising (probability 0.182)—chance alone is a reasonable explanation.

choices.text: The sample proportion actually contradicted the alternative hypothesis
choices.feedback: The data leaned in the direction of $H_a$, but not strongly enough to rule out chance.

choices.text: We proved that the college's marijuana use rate equals the national rate
choices.feedback: We can never accept $H_0$; we simply lack evidence against it.

model.hint: Think about how much sample proportions vary in samples of only 100 students.

children.value: Check Your Understanding: How the Significance Level Affects Conclusions

children.label: Check Your Understanding: How the Significance Level Affects Conclusions

children.value: Two hypothesis tests were conducted. In test I, a significance level of 0.05 was used, and the p-value was calculated to be 0.025. In test II, a significance level of 0.01 was used, and the p-value was calculated to be 0.025.

model.question: What is the conclusion of test I?

choices.text: Reject $H_0—the$ results are statistically significant at the 0.05 level
choices.feedback: Correct! $0.025 < 0.05$, so the results are significant and $H_0$ is rejected.

choices.text: Do not reject $H_0—the$ results are not statistically significant
choices.feedback: 0.025 is smaller than the significance level 0.05, so $H_0$ IS rejected.

model.question: What is the conclusion of test II?

choices.text: Do not reject $H_0—the$ results are not statistically significant at the 0.01 level
choices.feedback: Correct! $0.025 > 0.01$, so at the stricter 0.01 level the data do not provide enough evidence to reject $H_0$.
At the 0.01 level, a p-value of 0.025 is NOT small enough to reject $H_0$.

model.question: The same p-value (0.025) led to different conclusions in tests I and II. What does this illustrate?

choices.text: The conclusion depends on the chosen significance level as well as the p-value
choices.feedback: Correct! The conclusion depends not only on the strength of the evidence (the p-value) but also on how demanding a standard of evidence $(\alpha)$ we choose before the test.

choices.text: The two tests must have had different p-values
choices.feedback: The p-value was identical in both tests—what differed was the significance level.

choices.text: One of the two tests must have been done incorrectly
choices.feedback: Neither test was done incorrectly; different fields legitimately use different significance levels.

model.hint: The p-value measures the evidence; $\alpha$ is the standard we hold that evidence to.

children.value: The 0.05 significance level has no deep mathematical justification—it is a convention that has proven practical: strict enough to screen out most chance findings, lenient enough that real effects of reasonable size can be detected with realistic sample sizes. When the consequences of a false rejection are serious (for example, approving a new drug), researchers often use a stricter level such as 0.01. The important thing is to choose the significance level
